slides.title: Spelling patterns
slides.text:
Many words follow **patterns**. If you know the pattern, you can spell many words.

b**ack**, s**ack**, tr**ack**

slides.title: ck after a short vowel
slides.text:
After a **short vowel**, the k sound at the end is often **ck**.

d**uck**, cl**ock**, st**ick**

After a consonant, use **k**: mil**k**, des**k**.

slides.title: Double l, s, f
slides.text:
After a short vowel in a short word, we often **double** l, s or f at the end.

be**ll**, mi**ss**, cli**ff**

hi**ll**, gla**ss**, pu**ff**

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Read each sentence.
2. Look at the end of each short word.
3. Ask: Does it follow the pattern? Short vowel + ck? Short vowel + ll, ss or ff?

The sentence with the word that breaks the pattern is your proof.

example.explain: **bel** breaks the pattern. A short word with a short vowel doubles the l: **bell**.

together.passage: My cat is black. She sat on a rok. She saw a duck. She ran up the hill.
together.hint: Look at words that end with the k sound. Is there a short vowel before it?
together.good: Yes! rock has a short o, so the k sound is spelled ck.

evidence.stem: Tap the sentence with the word that breaks the pattern.
evidence.wrong: The words in this sentence follow the pattern. Look again.

checks.passage: Sami fell in the mud. He got a big mes on his shirt.
checks.why: mess is a short word with a short e, so the s is doubled.

checks.passage: The ship has a big deck.
checks.stem: Why does deck end in ck?
options: Short vowel before the k sound.
checks.why: deck has a short e before the k sound, so it ends in ck.

checks.passage: We went up a tall clif.
checks.why: cliff has a short i, so the f is doubled.

again.title: Short and quick
again.text:
Say the word. Is the vowel **short and quick**, like in **cat**, **bed**, **sit**, **hot** or **cup**?

Then the ending is often **ck**, **ll**, **ss** or **ff**.
again.example:
d-u-? (a bird that swims) → short u → **duck**

b-e-? (it rings) → short e → **bell**

slides.title: Silent e
slides.text:
A **silent e** at the end makes the vowel say its **name**.

hop → hop**e**
cut → cut**e**
bit → bit**e**

slides.title: Adding -ing or -ed to silent e words
slides.text:
**Drop** the silent e before adding -ing or -ed.

hope → hop**ing**
make → mak**ing**
smile → smil**ed**

slides.title: Doubling the last letter
slides.text:
If a short word ends in **one short vowel + one consonant**, **double** the consonant before -ing or -ed.

hop → ho**pp**ing
stop → sto**pp**ed
run → ru**nn**ing

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find words with -ing or -ed.
2. Think of the base word: hop or hope?
3. Silent e? Drop it. Short vowel + one consonant? Double it.

Point to the sentence where the rule is broken.

sentences.t: The rabbit was hopping across the grass.
A girl was hoping to catch it.

example.explain:
**hopping** comes from **hop** (short o), so the p is doubled.

**hoping** comes from **hope**, so the e is dropped. Two different words!

together.passage: Yesterday, my little brother and I were making a model car. He was cuting the paper wheels. I was gluing them onto a box. When we finished, we smiled at our work.
together.hint: Find the base word of each -ing word. Which one has a short vowel and one consonant at the end?
together.good: Yes! cut has a short u and ends in one t, so we double it: cutting.

sentences: Yesterday, my little brother and I were making a model car.
He was cuting the paper wheels.
I was gluing them onto a box.
When we finished, we smiled at our work.
evidence.stem: Tap the sentence where the spelling rule is broken.
evidence.wrong: The -ing and -ed words here follow the rules. Look for a base word that needed doubling.

checks.passage: The bus stoped at the corner.
checks.why: stop has a short o and one p at the end, so the p doubles: stopped.

checks.passage: Noura is writing a letter to her grandmother.
checks.stem: Why is there only one t in writing?
options: Write has a silent e, which is dropped.
checks.why: write ends in a silent e. We drop the e and add -ing, with no doubling: writing.

checks.passage: We were runing in the park.
checks.why: run has a short u and ends in one n, so the n doubles: running.

again.title: Look at the end
again.text:
Look at the base word's end.

**Short vowel + one consonant** (hop, sit, run) → double it: hopping.

**Silent e** (hope, bite, make) → drop it: hoping.
again.example:
swim + ing → short i + m → **swimming**

ride + ing → silent e → **riding**

slides.title: Double consonants in the middle
slides.text:
In many two-syllable words, a **short vowel** is followed by a **double consonant**.

ra**bb**it, ha**pp**en, di**nn**er, su**mm**er, li**tt**le

Split the word: rab·bit, hap·pen. Each syllable gets one of the letters.

slides.title: Single or double?
slides.text:
If the first vowel is **long**, there is usually only **one** consonant.

ti**g**er (ti·ger), pa**p**er (pa·per)

Short vowel → often double: di**nn**er.
Long vowel → single: di**n**er.

slides.title: More regular patterns
slides.text:
After a short vowel: **-dge** and **-tch** (bri**dge**, ba**dge**, ca**tch**, ki**tch**en)

After a long vowel or a consonant: **-ge** and **-ch** (pa**ge**, hu**ge**, bea**ch**, lun**ch**)

**-ight** spells long i: n**ight**, br**ight**, fl**ight**

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the word that looks wrong.
2. Split it into syllables and listen to the first vowel.
3. Short vowel → often a double consonant or -dge/-tch. Long vowel → usually single.

The sentence with the word that breaks the pattern is your proof.

sentences.t: After dinner, we walked across the old stone bridge.
The bright moon was shining over the river.

example.explain:
**dinner**: short i, so double n. **bridge**: short i, so **-dge**. **bright**: long i spelled **-ight**.

All of them follow regular patterns.

together.passage: Every summer, my family visits a small farm near Taif. My cousins and I feed the rabbits and collect eggs from the chickens. In the afternoon, we help in the kichen. My aunt bakes fresh bread, and we spread butter and honey on it. At night, we sit outside and look at the bright stars.
together.hint: Look for a short vowel followed by the ch sound. Which pattern should it use?
together.good: Yes! kitchen has a short i before the ch sound, so it is spelled with -tch.

sentences: Every summer, my family visits a small farm near Taif.
My cousins and I feed the rabbits and collect eggs from the chickens.
In the afternoon, we help in the kichen.
My aunt bakes fresh bread, and we spread butter and honey on it.
At night, we sit outside and look at the bright stars.
evidence.stem: Tap the sentence with the misspelled word.
evidence.wrong: The words in this sentence follow the regular patterns. Keep looking.

checks.passage: Something strange hapened on the way to school.
checks.why: hap·pen has a short a, so the p is doubled: happened.

checks.passage: The tiger rested under a tree.
checks.stem: Why does tiger have only one g?
options: The i in ti·ger is short.
The i in ti·ger is long.
checks.why: The i says its name (long i), so only one consonant follows it.

checks.passage: The goalkeeper made an amazing cach.
checks.why: catch has a short a before the ch sound, so it uses -tch.

again.title: Listen to the first vowel
again.text:
Say the first part of the word.

Short, quick vowel (like in **hat**) → expect a **double** consonant or **-tch / -dge**.

Long vowel that says its name (like in **hate**) → expect a **single** consonant.
again.example:
ha_y (glad) → short a → **happy**

pa_er (you write on it) → long a → **paper**

slides.title: Doubling in longer words
slides.text:
In words of two or more syllables, double the final consonant only if the **last syllable is stressed**.

be**GIN** → begi**nn**ing
pre**FER** → prefe**rr**ed

If the stress comes earlier, do not double:
**VIS**it → visi**t**ing, **O**pen → ope**n**ed

slides.title: Words that break the rules
slides.text:
Some common words do not follow regular patterns. Learn them by sight:

**said, once, busy, women, ocean, enough, island, answer**

Their letters do not match the way they sound.

slides.title: Silent letters and odd groups
slides.text:
**kn**: knee, knife
**wr**: write, wrong
**ough** sounds different in though, through, enough and thought
**s** in island, **w** in answer

Many of these come from older forms of English.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the word that looks wrong.
2. Decide: is it a regular-pattern word or a rule-breaker?
3. Regular → check the pattern (stress and doubling, silent e).
4. Rule-breaker → compare it with the spelling you learned by sight.

Point to the sentence that holds the error.

sentences.t: The race was beginning, and the runners were ready.
Coach Faisal was visiting from another school.
He said the race would be close.

example.explain:
**beginning**: the stress is on the last syllable (be·GIN), so the n doubles.

**visiting**: the stress is on the first syllable (VIS·it), so the t does not double.

together.passage: Last spring, our class went on a trip to an island in the Red Sea. We traveled by boat, and the ocean was calm and clear. Our guide, a marine scientist, answered many of our questions. She explained that the coral reefs were in danger and that people must protect them. Some students said they had never seen so many colorful fish. By the time we left, everyone agreed they prefered this trip to any other.
together.hint: Find a word with -ed. Where is the stress in its base word?
together.good: Yes! pre·FER is stressed on the last syllable, so the r doubles: preferred.

sentences: Last spring, our class went on a trip to an island in the Red Sea.
We traveled by boat, and the ocean was calm and clear.
Our guide, a marine scientist, answered many of our questions.
She explained that the coral reefs were in danger and that people must protect them.
Some students said they had never seen so many colorful fish.
By the time we left, everyone agreed they prefered this trip to any other.
evidence.stem: Tap the sentence with the misspelled word.
evidence.wrong: The words here are spelled correctly, including the rule-breakers island, ocean and answered.

checks.passage: We admited that we had made a mistake.
checks.why: ad·MIT is stressed on the last syllable, so the t doubles: admitted.

checks.passage: I have enuf money to buy the book.
checks.why: enough is a rule-breaker. Its f sound is spelled gh, so it must be learned by sight.

checks.passage: Fahad opened the window to let in the cool air.
checks.stem: Why is there only one n in opened?
options: The stress is on the first syllable: O·pen.
The stress is on the last syllable: o·PEN.
checks.why: The stress falls on O, not on the last syllable, so the n is not doubled.

again.title: Tap out the stress
again.text:
Say the word and **tap the table** on the loudest syllable.

Loudest at the **end** (be·GIN) → double before -ing or -ed.

Loudest at the **start** (VIS·it) → do not double.
again.example:
for·GET + ing → loud at the end → **forgetting**

LIS·ten + ing → loud at the start → **listening**
